question: How do continuous-improvement model version control and logging tests work together in the technical standard?
draft:
The available excerpts establish both mechanisms as separate requirements within the Australian Government AI Technical Standard, but do not describe an explicit interaction or integration between them.

**Model version control (continuous improvement frameworks)**

Under Statement 25 (Implement continuous improvement frameworks), agencies must perform model version control [3]. AI model versioning and tracking is described as key to comparing performance over time, identifying factors affecting performance, and updating the model when needed [3]. Model tracking and versioning can involve dataset tracking and versioning, and model tracking and versioning — with each trained model potentially carrying details such as algorithm, learning type and hyperparameter settings, compile-time parameters, and the tools or version of tools used to compile the model [3]. The statement also directs setting up rollback options to historical models to help develop safety nets, reduce risk of deploying new models, and provide deployment flexibility [3]. Statement 25 additionally requires establishing interface tools and feedback channels for machines and humans, including appropriate human-machine interface tools for human interrogation and oversight [3].

**Logging tests**

Under Statement 27 (Test for specified behaviour), agencies must perform logging tests as per the requirements [5]. This involves verifying that the system records system warnings and errors, and relevant system changes with corresponding details of who made the change, timestamp, and system version [5].

**Synthesis (not stated as an integrated requirement in the excerpts)**

The two provisions are adjacent in function: logging tests verify that the system records the system version alongside change details [5], while model version control requires tracking model versions and their attributes and retaining rollback options [3]. Read together, the logging-test criterion supplies the evidentiary record (who changed what, when, and under which system version) that version-control tracking depends on. However, the excerpts do not state that logging tests are the mechanism for verifying version control, nor do they establish any cross-reference, sequencing, or dependency between Statement 25 and Statement 27.

**Evidence gaps**

The provided excerpts do not establish an explicit linkage, shared procedure, or combined requirement connecting model version control and logging tests. Any relationship beyond their separate stated requirements is not supported by the retrieved evidence.

Key considerations when setting up a monitoring system include:

• What to log: Organisations should determine their objectives for monitoring (e.g. real -time intervention, debugging , integration between components ) to identify what to log. In doing so, prioritise monitoring for high -risk activities such as updating database records or financial transactions.

• How to effectively monitor logs: Organisations can consider implementing these practices:

o Monitor on multiple layers, such as the user-agent interaction, agent-tool invocation, and model reasoning layers to identify specific sources of failure.

child_citations.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
child_citations.quote:
4. Enable end-user responsibility

Trustworthy deployment of agents does not rely solely on developers, but also on end- users using them responsibly. To enable responsible use, as a baseline, users should be informed of the agent’s range of actions, access to data, and the user’s own responsibilities. Organisations should consider layering on training to equip employees with the knowledge required to manage human-agent interactions and exercise effective oversight, while maintaining their tradecraft and foundational skills.

This is a living document. We have worked with government agencies and leading companies to collate current best practices and contribute real- world case studies, but this is a fast-developing space. This framework will need to be continuously updated to keep pace with new developments. We invite feedback to refine the framework, and more case studies demonstrating how the framework can be applied for responsible agentic deployment.

What’s new in this version

This version incorporates feedback received from 60+ companies since v1.0. The main changes include:

Introduction to Agentic AI What is Agentic

AI? • Agentic components: Added safety and reliability components (controls, logging and monitoring) as part of agent’s core components • Protocols: Updated for newer protocols, especially for agentic commerce Risks of Agentic AI • Systemic and multi-agent risks: Added systemic and multi-agent risks

The four dimensions • Case study from IMDA on how the framework can be applied to OpenClaw deployments
